data.title: My First React Component
data.description:
Welcome to your first React challenge! Your task is to build a simple welcome interface for the application. Design a standalone `Welcome` component that introduces the app, featuring a primary heading

with the text 'Welcome to React', followed by a descriptive paragraph

saying 'This is my first React application.'. Finally, ensure that this welcome interface is successfully integrated and displayed on the main application screen.

requirements.text: Component name must be Welcome.
Must render an h1 with text 'Welcome to React'.
Must render a paragraph with text 'This is my first React application.'
requirements.expectedValue: This is my first React application.

requirements.text: App component must render Welcome.

data.title: Rendering HTML in React
data.description:
In this exercise, you will initialize and render a React application to the DOM. Your objective is to use the standard React 18 DOM client API to mount a specific UI structure into the existing root element. Create a container element assigned the class `root-card`. Inside this card, display a primary heading

containing the exact text 'React Root Node', followed by a short paragraph

stating 'Learning createRoot()'. Render this entire UI block to see it appear on the screen!

requirements.text: Must use createRoot from react-dom/client.
Must render a div with className 'root-card'.
Must render an h1 with text 'React Root Node'.
Must render a paragraph with text 'Learning createRoot()'.

data.title: JSX className Attribute
data.description: Your task is to build a user profile card. Create a new component called `Profile` that presents two pieces of information: the user's role ('Frontend Developer') and their current activity ('Learning JSX'). To ensure the card is styled correctly by our pre-written stylesheet, you must apply the CSS class named `profile` to the component's outermost wrapping element using the appropriate JSX syntax. Finally, integrate and display this profile card within the main `App` component.

requirements.text: Component name must be Profile.
Must use className='profile' on the wrapper element.
Must display 'Frontend Developer'.
Must display the text 'Learning JSX'.

data.title: JSX Expressions with Variables
data.description: Let's bring your UI to life with dynamic data! Your task is to build a profile card by embedding JavaScript variables directly into your markup. First, define two variables inside your component: a `name` (string) and an `age` (number). Next, design the card's layout: use a primary heading <h1> to display the user's name, followed by two separate text elements. The first should state 'Age: ' along with the current age. The second must display 'Age Next Year: ' followed by their calculated age for the upcoming year. **Crucial:** You must calculate the future age using a math operation within a JSX expression—hardcoded values will not pass! Finally, wrap your entire profile layout inside a container element with the `user-profile` class.

requirements.text: Must declare the variable 'name'.
Must declare the variable 'age'.
Must render name in an h1 using a JSX expression.
Must display Age Next Year computed as age + 1.

data.title: Interactive Profile Card
data.description:
Let's level up the profile card by adding interactivity and practicing different ways to assign JSX attributes! Build a `ProfileCard` component that includes a title ('Frontend Developer'), a short description ('Learning React JSX Attributes'), and two action buttons. 

**Styling Rules:** Apply the CSS class `profile-heading` to your title. For the main card wrapper, you must define a variable named `cardClass` holding the string `'profile-card'` and pass it dynamically to the wrapper's class attribute. Please rely on the provided CSS classes; do NOT use inline styles.

**Interactivity:** The first button, labeled 'Show Message', must trigger a browser alert displaying exactly 'Hello React!' when clicked. The second button, labeled 'Coming Soon', must be rendered in a disabled state.

requirements.text: Must declare and use the 'cardClass' variable as className.
Show Message button must call alert('Hello React!') on click.
Coming Soon button must be disabled.
Heading must use the CSS class 'profile-heading'.

data.title: Styling React Components
data.description: Time to make the profile card look professional using CSS classes! Your task is to style the `ProfileCard` component that displays information for 'Alex Johnson', a 'Frontend Developer' who is 'Learning React Styling'. Using the pre-defined stylesheet, apply the following design rules: First, wrap the entire component's content in a container using the `card-container` class. Next, format the user's name as a prominent title by applying the `profile-heading` class to it. Finally, draw attention to the current learning status ('Learning React Styling') by applying the `highlight-text` class to that specific element. Note: Inline styles are strictly prohibited in this exercise—you must rely entirely on JSX class attributes!

requirements.text: Component name must be ProfileCard.
Must use CSS class 'card-container'.
Must use CSS class 'profile-heading'.
Must use CSS class 'highlight-text'.

data.title: React CSS Modules
data.description: Let's explore scoped styling to prevent class name collisions! Your objective is to craft a reusable `Button` component that displays the text 'Click Me' and style it using CSS Modules. First, open the `Button.module.css` file and design a custom class from scratch—give it a solid background color, comfortable padding, rounded corners, and an interactive hover state. Once your design is ready, switch over to `Button.jsx`, import this stylesheet as a module, and dynamically bind your custom class to the button element. Keep your component clean: inline styles are strictly prohibited!

code_test.css: body { margin: 0; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; height: 100vh; background-color: #0f172a; font-family: 'Inter', -apple-system, sans-serif; }

requirements.text: Component name must be Button.
Must import styles from './Button.module.css'.
Must apply className to the button element.
Button must display the text 'Click Me'.

data.title: React JSX Conditional Statements
data.description:
It's time to build a dynamic UI feature! Your task is to develop a `StatusBadge` component that indicates whether a user is currently active. The component must accept a boolean prop named `isOnline` (which should default to true). Based on this prop, the badge needs to update both its appearance and its text dynamically: when online, it should display 'Online' and use the `badge-online` CSS class; when offline, it should display 'Offline' and use the `badge-offline` CSS class.

**Strict Coding Standard:** To keep the React component clean and declarative, traditional `if/else` statements are strictly banned in this exercise. You must handle the conditional logic for both the text content and the `className` attribute by using inline ternary operators (`condition ? true : false`) directly within your JSX.

requirements.text: Create a React component named StatusBadge.
Accept a boolean prop called isOnline.
Use ternary (? :) to change className based on isOnline.
Use ternary (? :) to display 'Online' or 'Offline'.

data.title: React Component
data.description: Welcome to Milestone 3! Your objective is to build a foundational piece of UI. Create a functional component named `Greeting` that presents a prominent welcome message displaying exactly 'Hello, React!'. Because this component is purely presentational and only renders static content, it must remain entirely stateless—do not use any React hooks here. Once your component is ready, integrate it into the main application layout by rendering it inside the provided container element styled with the `card` class.

requirements.text: Component name must be Greeting.
Component must return an h1 element.
The h1 must contain the text 'Hello, React!'.

data.title: Passing Props
data.description:
Let's make our components reusable by passing data into them! Your task is to build a `UserCard` component that receives external data and displays it. The component needs to accept a property named `username` and render a level-3 heading with the exact format 'User: [provided username]'. 

**Core Rules:**
1. **Prop Handling:** To master the fundamentals of how React passes data, you must receive the data via the standard `props` object parameter and access the `username` property directly from it. **Do not use object destructuring** in the function signature.
2. **Stateless:** Keep the component purely presentational—React hooks are strictly prohibited.

Finally, mount your `UserCard` inside the main `App` component's container and pass a sample name (like 'Alex') to see your dynamic component in action!

requirements.text: Component name must be UserCard.
Component must accept a prop named username via props object.
Component must return an h3 element.
The h3 must contain 'User: ' followed by the username value.

data.title: Destructuring Props - Default Values
data.description:
Let's write cleaner code by leveraging destructuring! Your objective is to build a `Product` component that displays merchandise details based on three incoming properties: `name`, `price`, and `category`.

**Core Requirements:**
- **Destructuring & Defaults:** You must extract these properties directly within the function parameter list (do not use the `props` object inside the function body). Since some products might not be categorized yet, assign a fallback default value of `'General'` for the `category` prop.
- **UI Layout:** Wrap the product details in a container using the `product-card` CSS class. Inside this card, display the product's name as a heading, its price in a paragraph (make sure to prepend a `$` symbol to the number), and the category in a `span` element.
- **Module Export:** The test suite requires you to export the `Product` component as a **named export** (not a default export). As always for presentational components, do not use any React hooks.

requirements.text: Component name must be Product.
Must use props destructuring in function parameters.
Must set default value 'General' for category.
Must export Product as a named export.

data.title: Stateful Counter Component
data.description:
Let's bring interactivity to your React components using state! Your challenge is to build a `Counter` component that tracks and displays a number, starting at zero. You must use the `useState` hook to manage this dynamic data.

**UI Requirements:** Wrap the entire component in a container using the `counter-container` class, and display the current count prominently as a primary heading. Below the number, provide three action buttons grouped together in a wrapper with the `btn-group` class.

**Behavior & Styling:** The buttons must be logically labeled 'Decrement', 'Reset', and 'Increment'. Wire them up so they correctly decrease the count by 1, reset the count to 0, and increase the count by 1, respectively. Don't forget to apply their corresponding CSS classes (`btn-decrement`, `btn-reset`, `btn-increment`) to ensure they match our design system!

requirements.text: Component name must be Counter.
Must use the useState hook.
Increment button must increase count by 1.
Decrement button must decrease count by 1.
Reset button must set count back to 0.
